founderScope: 100 draft demos; no publish authorization; empirical claims unverified

entries.title: Par or birdie?
entries.hook: Does the same-length putt carry the same pressure?
entries.objective: Separate an observational scoring difference from a claim that pressure caused it.
entries.sourceText: PGA pros sink par putts a few percentage points more often than equally long birdie putts, because missing par feels like a loss (Pope & Schweitzer, 2011).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate an observational scoring difference from a claim that pressure caused it.

entries.title: One second before four hours
entries.hook: Would a round-number finish change the pace you choose?
entries.objective: Recognize bunching just below a round-number target in a finish-time distribution.
entries.sourceText: Marathon finishing times bunch just under round numbers like 4:00, which act as reference points (Allen, Dechow, Pope & Wu, 2017).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Recognize bunching just below a round-number target in a finish-time distribution.

entries.title: The price you paid
entries.hook: Should your old purchase price change today's listing?
entries.objective: Distinguish a seller's historical reference point from the current market offer.
entries.sourceText: Boston condo owners facing a nominal loss set higher asking prices and waited longer to sell (Genesove & Mayer, 2001).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish a seller's historical reference point from the current market offer.

entries.title: Check daily or yearly?
entries.hook: Would you choose the same portfolio after changing the reporting interval?
entries.objective: Explain how aggregating returns changes how often a loss appears without changing the assets.
entries.sourceText: People shown investment results less often put more money in stocks (Gneezy & Potters, 1997; Thaler, Tversky, Kahneman & Schwartz, 1997).
entries.sourcePointer: 500-behavioral-economics-findings.md entry 16: Gneezy & Potters, 1997; Thaler, Tversky, Kahneman & Schwartz, 1997
entries.meaningfulDifference: Explain how aggregating returns changes how often a loss appears without changing the assets.

entries.title: An expert sees the listing
entries.hook: Does professional experience remove a visible price anchor?
entries.objective: Compare an appraisal made with a listing price against one made without it.
entries.sourceText: Real estate agents' appraisals shifted with the listing price they were shown, though most denied using it (Northcraft & Neale, 1987).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare an appraisal made with a listing price against one made without it.

entries.title: A precise opening offer
entries.hook: Would $4,988 and $5,000 invite the same counteroffer?
entries.objective: Identify opening-price precision as distinct from the opening-price level.
entries.sourceText: Precise opening prices like $4,988 draw smaller counteroffers than round ones like $5,000 (Janiszewski & Uy, 2008; Mason et al., 2013).
entries.sourcePointer: 500-behavioral-economics-findings.md entry 29: Janiszewski & Uy, 2008; Mason et al., 2013
entries.meaningfulDifference: Identify opening-price precision as distinct from the opening-price level.

entries.title: Make the opposite case
entries.hook: What happens if you list reasons the suggested price could be wrong?
entries.objective: Contrast attending to an anchor with deliberately retrieving disconfirming evidence.
entries.sourceText: Car experts' price estimates were anchored too; asking them to consider why the anchor was wrong reduced the bias (Mussweiler, Strack & Pfeiffer, 2000).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast attending to an anchor with deliberately retrieving disconfirming evidence.

entries.title: The suggested donation
entries.hook: Does changing suggested amounts change your chosen gift?
entries.objective: Distinguish a donation suggestion from a minimum requirement and inspect the response distribution.
entries.sourceText: Suggested amounts in fundraising pull donations toward them (Edwards & List, 2014).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish a donation suggestion from a minimum requirement and inspect the response distribution.

entries.title: Lean or fat?
entries.hook: Would you rate the same package differently after flipping the label?
entries.objective: Translate complementary attribute labels without changing the underlying composition.
entries.sourceText: Ground beef labeled "75% lean" was rated tastier and less greasy than "25% fat" (Levin & Gaeth, 1988).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Translate complementary attribute labels without changing the underlying composition.

entries.title: What is this game called?
entries.hook: Would calling the same choices a community game change your play?
entries.objective: Separate a game's label from its unchanged payoff table.
entries.sourceText: The same prisoner's dilemma called the "Community Game" drew about twice the cooperation as when called the "Wall Street Game" (Liberman, Samuels & Ross, 2004).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate a game's label from its unchanged payoff table.

entries.title: Which car saves more fuel?
entries.hook: Which mileage upgrade saves more fuel over the same distance?
entries.objective: Compute fuel saved per distance rather than comparing miles-per-gallon differences.
entries.sourceText: People misjudge fuel savings in miles per gallon; gallons per 100 miles fixes the illusion (Larrick & Soll, 2008).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compute fuel saved per distance rather than comparing miles-per-gallon differences.

entries.title: Bonus or rebate?
entries.hook: Would you spend the same $50 if its label changed?
entries.objective: Compare windfall and refund descriptions while holding available cash fixed.
entries.sourceText: People spent more of a $50 payment framed as a "bonus" than one framed as a "rebate" ($22 vs $9.55) (Epley, Mak & Idson, 2006).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare windfall and refund descriptions while holding available cash fixed.

entries.title: Registered or donated?
entries.hook: Do donor-registration rates tell us the actual donation gap?
entries.objective: Separate a participation proxy from the downstream clinical outcome in country comparisons.
entries.sourceText: Presumed-consent countries have roughly 25–30% higher actual donation rates, a smaller gap than registration suggests (Abadie & Gay, 2006).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate a participation proxy from the downstream clinical outcome in country comparisons.

entries.title: Pick your own starting point
entries.hook: What if the form requires a decision instead of supplying one?
entries.objective: Distinguish active choice from opt-in and opt-out enrollment.
entries.sourceText: Requiring new hires to actively choose raised participation about 28 percentage points versus opt-in (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2009).
entries.sourcePointer: 500-behavioral-economics-findings.md entry 67: Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2009
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish active choice from opt-in and opt-out enrollment.

entries.title: The printer starts one-sided
entries.hook: How much paper could a default change save in this print queue?
entries.objective: Trace a duplex setting through sheet counts while leaving document content fixed.
entries.sourceText: Switching a Swedish university's printers to double-sided by default cut paper use about 15% (Egebark & Ekström, 2016).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Trace a duplex setting through sheet counts while leaving document content fixed.

entries.title: Who chose the default?
entries.hook: Would you read a preselected option as advice or as convenience?
entries.objective: Distinguish perceived recommendation from mechanical effort when interpreting a default.
entries.sourceText: People read defaults as an implicit recommendation from whoever set them (McKenzie, Liersch & Finkelstein, 2006).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish perceived recommendation from mechanical effort when interpreting a default.

entries.title: Pay monthly or per visit?
entries.hook: At this month's attendance, which gym contract costs less?
entries.objective: Compare realized cost per visit with a pay-per-visit alternative.
entries.sourceText: Gym members on monthly contracts paid over $70 a month but went about 4.3 times, roughly $17 a visit, when a $10 day pass was available (DellaVigna & Malmendier, 2006).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare realized cost per visit with a pay-per-visit alternative.

entries.title: Who sets the deadline?
entries.hook: Would you choose one final deadline or several costly checkpoints?
entries.objective: Compare self-imposed deadlines with externally spaced deadlines without claiming a universal best schedule.
entries.sourceText: Students set themselves costly deadlines, but evenly spaced imposed deadlines produced the best work (Ariely & Wertenbroch, 2002).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare self-imposed deadlines with externally spaced deadlines without claiming a universal best schedule.

entries.title: A book only at the gym
entries.hook: What changes when a tempting audiobook is available only during exercise?
entries.objective: Identify temptation bundling and distinguish its early effect from sustained adherence.
entries.sourceText: Allowing gym-goers to hear tempting audiobooks only at the gym raised visits 51% at first (Milkman, Minson & Volpp, 2014).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Identify temptation bundling and distinguish its early effect from sustained adherence.

entries.title: Order on a cold day
entries.hook: Would today's weather change what you want from next month's coat?
entries.objective: Contrast the purchase-day state with the later consumption-day state in a projection-bias example.
entries.sourceText: Cold-weather clothing ordered on unusually cold days was returned more often (Conlin, O'Donoghue & Vogelsang, 2007).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast the purchase-day state with the later consumption-day state in a projection-bias example.

entries.title: The fuel budget shrinks
entries.hook: If fuel gets cheaper, would you buy more premium gasoline?
entries.objective: Separate a general income increase from spending inside a labeled fuel account.
entries.sourceText: When gas prices fell, US households upgraded to premium gasoline far more than the income gain would predict (Hastings & Shapiro, 2013).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate a general income increase from spending inside a labeled fuel account.

entries.title: Just paid for the gym
entries.hook: Should elapsed time since payment affect the value of the next visit?
entries.objective: Separate payment timing from the marginal physical benefit of attendance.
entries.sourceText: Gym attendance peaks just after a payment and fades until the next one (Gourville & Soman, 1998).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate payment timing from the marginal physical benefit of attendance.

entries.title: Card or cash for tickets?
entries.hook: Would changing the payment method change your maximum bid?
entries.objective: Compare willingness to pay under payment methods while holding the ticket fixed.
entries.sourceText: MBA students bid up to twice as much for Celtics tickets when paying by credit card instead of cash (Prelec & Simester, 2001).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare willingness to pay under payment methods while holding the ticket fixed.

entries.title: Wages in two envelopes
entries.hook: Would separating the same wages change how much you save?
entries.objective: Track partitioned balances without treating labeling as additional income.
entries.sourceText: Indian laborers saved more when wages were split into sealed envelopes, especially envelopes showing their children's photos (Soman & Cheema, 2011).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Track partitioned balances without treating labeling as additional income.

entries.title: The experienced trader's mug
entries.hook: Should market experience change the gap between buying and selling prices?
entries.objective: Contrast ownership valuation across experience groups rather than asserting a universal endowment ratio.
entries.sourceText: Experienced sports-card dealers showed little endowment effect (List, 2003).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast ownership valuation across experience groups rather than asserting a universal endowment ratio.

entries.title: Look, or pick it up?
entries.hook: Would touching an item change your valuation before you own it?
entries.objective: Distinguish physical contact and perceived ownership from legal ownership.
entries.sourceText: Just touching an object raises the feeling of ownership and its value (Peck & Shu, 2009).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish physical contact and perceived ownership from legal ownership.

entries.title: You built this shelf
entries.hook: Would assembling the item change your asking price for it?
entries.objective: Separate production effort from the resulting item's externally matched quality.
entries.sourceText: People value furniture they assembled themselves more than identical pre-built items, the "IKEA effect" (Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 2012).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate production effort from the resulting item's externally matched quality.

entries.title: Regret now, regret later
entries.hook: Would your worst regret change if we asked next year?
entries.objective: Distinguish short-term action regret from longer-term inaction regret.
entries.sourceText: Actions are regretted more in the short run (Kahneman & Tversky, 1982), but inactions more over a lifetime (Gilovich & Medvec, 1995).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish short-term action regret from longer-term inaction regret.

entries.title: A second good option
entries.hook: Would adding another attractive player make buying easier?
entries.objective: Show how choice conflict can change deferral while both options remain available.
entries.sourceText: With one good CD player on sale, 34% chose to wait; adding a second good option raised waiting to 46% (Tversky & Shafir, 1992).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Show how choice conflict can change deferral while both options remain available.

entries.title: Information or form help?
entries.hook: Is knowing aid exists the same as completing its application?
entries.objective: Distinguish an information intervention from assistance that removes application steps.
entries.sourceText: Having tax preparers fill out the FAFSA aid form raised college enrollment from 28% to 36% (Bettinger, Long, Oreopoulos & Sanbonmatsu, 2012).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish an information intervention from assistance that removes application steps.

entries.title: A personalized comparison
entries.hook: Would a letter using your own drug costs change your plan search?
entries.objective: Contrast generic plan information with a personalized alternative comparison.
entries.sourceText: Personalized letters comparing Medicare drug plans led 28% to switch versus 17% of controls (Kling et al., 2012).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast generic plan information with a personalized alternative comparison.

entries.title: Who comes first on the ballot?
entries.hook: Would an identical candidate gain from moving to the first row?
entries.objective: Separate presentation order from candidate attributes and note the low-information context.
entries.sourceText: Candidates listed first on ballots gain votes, especially in low-information races (Koppell & Steen, 2004).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate presentation order from candidate attributes and note the low-information context.

entries.title: The same split in two societies
entries.hook: Is one laboratory's usual offer a human universal?
entries.objective: Read cross-society variation without treating one observed average as a fixed preference.
entries.sourceText: Across 15 small-scale societies, mean offers ranged from 26% among the Machiguenga to 58% among the Lamalera (Henrich et al., 2001).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Read cross-society variation without treating one observed average as a fixed preference.

entries.title: You can give, or take
entries.hook: Does adding a take option change what a donation means?
entries.objective: Inspect how the feasible choice set changes the interpretation of zero giving.
entries.sourceText: Adding an option to take money from the recipient sharply cuts giving (List, 2007; Bardsley, 2008).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Inspect how the feasible choice set changes the interpretation of zero giving.

entries.title: Leave the consequences hidden
entries.hook: Would you pay attention to how your choice affects the other player?
entries.objective: Distinguish choosing under ignorance from choosing after learning the consequence.
entries.sourceText: When people could avoid learning how their choice affected others, fair choices roughly halved (Dana, Weber & Kuang, 2007).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish choosing under ignorance from choosing after learning the consequence.

entries.title: Same gap, a visible reason
entries.hook: Does a pay difference feel different when productivity differences are visible?
entries.objective: Compare unequal pay with and without observable performance justification.
entries.sourceText: Indian workers paid less than peers cut output and attendance, unless the pay gap matched visible productivity differences (Breza, Kaur & Shamdasani, 2018).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare unequal pay with and without observable performance justification.

entries.title: Who gets punished?
entries.hook: Could punishment harm cooperation if high contributors are targeted?
entries.objective: Distinguish punishment of free riders from punishment of cooperators.
entries.sourceText: In some cities, players punish the cooperators, not just free riders, which wrecks cooperation (Herrmann, Thöni & Gächter, 2008).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish punishment of free riders from punishment of cooperators.

entries.title: How long does a gift last?
entries.hook: Does an effort increase in hour one tell us what happens all day?
entries.objective: Separate an immediate gift-exchange response from its persistence over a work shift.
entries.sourceText: In real jobs, the effort boost from a surprise raise faded within hours (Gneezy & List, 2006).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate an immediate gift-exchange response from its persistence over a work shift.

entries.title: Talk before choosing
entries.hook: What could a conversation change when the payoff table stays fixed?
entries.objective: Distinguish communication from changes to material incentives in a social dilemma.
entries.sourceText: Letting players talk before a social dilemma sharply raises cooperation (Sally, 1995).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish communication from changes to material incentives in a social dilemma.

entries.title: More cash in the lost wallet
entries.hook: Would more money in a lost wallet make its return less likely?
entries.objective: Compare reported return outcomes by wallet condition without predicting an individual's honesty.
entries.sourceText: Across 40 countries, wallets with more money were returned more often: about 40% with none, 51% with $13.45 (Cohn, Maréchal, Tannenbaum & Zünd, 2019).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare reported return outcomes by wallet condition without predicting an individual's honesty.

entries.title: Already below the norm
entries.hook: Could a conservation message make a low-use household consume more?
entries.objective: Distinguish a descriptive average from an approval signal for already desirable behavior.
entries.sourceText: Low energy users told they were below average increased use, unless the report added a smiley face of approval (Schultz et al., 2007).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish a descriptive average from an approval signal for already desirable behavior.

entries.title: A warning that advertises theft
entries.hook: What does a theft warning imply about what other visitors do?
entries.objective: Contrast a descriptive norm about misconduct with an injunction against it.
entries.sourceText: A sign at Petrified Forest saying many visitors stole wood raised theft to 7.9%, versus 1.7% for a sign simply asking people not to take it (Cialdini, 2003).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast a descriptive norm about misconduct with an injunction against it.

entries.title: What do others really think?
entries.hook: Would correcting a mistaken social belief change a household's choice?
entries.objective: Distinguish private support from beliefs about others' support and the measured downstream action.
entries.sourceText: Most Saudi men privately supported women working outside the home but underestimated others' support; correcting this raised wives' job applications (Bursztyn, González & Yanagizawa-Drott, 2020).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish private support from beliefs about others' support and the measured downstream action.

entries.title: Who can see your work?
entries.hook: Would a fast colleague have the same effect if they could not observe you?
entries.objective: Separate proximity to a productive peer from being visible to that peer.
entries.sourceText: Supermarket cashiers worked faster when a highly productive colleague could see them (Mas & Moretti, 2009).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate proximity to a productive peer from being visible to that peer.

entries.title: Enter the skill contest?
entries.hook: Could confidence in your skill still lead to too much entry?
entries.objective: Distinguish absolute ability from ability relative to the competitors who also enter.
entries.sourceText: People enter competitions too often when success depends on their own skill, ignoring how good rivals are (Camerer & Lovallo, 1999).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish absolute ability from ability relative to the competitors who also enter.

entries.title: Write the forecast first
entries.hook: After seeing the result, how well can you remember your original forecast?
entries.objective: Compare a recorded prior forecast with a retrospective recollection.
entries.sourceText: After events, people believe they predicted them better than they did, the hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1975; Fischhoff & Beyth, 1975).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare a recorded prior forecast with a retrospective recollection.

entries.title: Your lottery ticket
entries.hook: Does choosing a ticket change its odds or just the price you demand?
entries.objective: Separate control over selection from control over a random outcome.
entries.sourceText: Office workers who chose their own lottery ticket asked $8.67 to sell it, versus $1.96 for those assigned one (Langer, 1975).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate control over selection from control over a random outcome.

entries.title: Read the case before your role
entries.hook: Would you judge the same facts differently after learning which side you represent?
entries.objective: Contrast evaluation before role assignment with self-serving interpretation afterward.
entries.sourceText: When negotiators read case facts before learning their role, settlements came much more easily than when they knew their side first (Babcock, Loewenstein, Issacharoff & Camerer, 1995).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast evaluation before role assignment with self-serving interpretation afterward.

entries.title: Where does K appear?
entries.hook: Are words beginning with K easier to find than words with K third?
entries.objective: Separate ease of retrieval from the frequency of the underlying class.
entries.sourceText: People think more words start with K than have K third, because first letters are easier to recall; the reverse is true (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate ease of retrieval from the frequency of the underlying class.

entries.title: A flood, then quiet years
entries.hook: Would flood-insurance demand stay high as the event recedes?
entries.objective: Distinguish the recent-event response from longer-run decay in attention.
entries.sourceText: Flood insurance take-up rises about 9% the year after a local flood, then falls back to baseline over roughly a decade (Gallagher, 2014).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish the recent-event response from longer-run decay in attention.

entries.title: The city you recognize
entries.hook: Can recognizing one city help when you cannot compare their populations?
entries.objective: Specify when a recognition heuristic can exploit informative environmental structure.
entries.sourceText: German students guessed which US city was larger better than Americans, by picking the one they recognized (Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Specify when a recognition heuristic can exploit informative environmental structure.

entries.title: How many birds are at stake?
entries.hook: Would your gift scale with a hundredfold change in the birds protected?
entries.objective: Compare scope-sensitive and scope-insensitive valuations without claiming every donor is insensitive.
entries.sourceText: People would pay about the same to save 2,000, 20,000 or 200,000 birds: $80, $78 and $88 (Desvousges et al., 1993).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare scope-sensitive and scope-insensitive valuations without claiming every donor is insensitive.

entries.title: Read the odds, or learn them
entries.hook: Would a rare loss matter equally after reading its odds and sampling outcomes?
entries.objective: Contrast described probabilities with experience that may omit rare outcomes.
entries.sourceText: Rare events are overweighted when described but underweighted when learned from experience (Hertwig, Barron, Weber & Erev, 2004).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast described probabilities with experience that may omit rare outcomes.

entries.title: Remove the final risk
entries.hook: Is eliminating a small risk valued like the same reduction elsewhere?
entries.objective: Distinguish zero-risk elimination from equal absolute risk reduction.
entries.sourceText: People pay a premium to remove a risk entirely rather than reduce it by the same amount (Viscusi, Magat & Huber, 1987).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish zero-risk elimination from equal absolute risk reduction.

entries.title: One person, six risk tests
entries.hook: Should one risk score predict all six of your choices?
entries.objective: Contrast domain-specific elicited risk preferences with a single stable risk ranking.
entries.sourceText: Risk preferences measured six different ways in the same people barely correlated (Pedroni et al., 2017).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast domain-specific elicited risk preferences with a single stable risk ranking.

entries.title: Who enters this tournament?
entries.hook: Would a gender difference in competition travel unchanged across societies?
entries.objective: Inspect reversal across social settings rather than interpreting one sample as biological destiny.
entries.sourceText: Women in matrilineal Khasi society chose to compete more often than men, the reverse of the patriarchal Maasai (Gneezy, Leonard & List, 2009).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Inspect reversal across social settings rather than interpreting one sample as biological destiny.

entries.title: One mile across the boundary
entries.hook: Should crossing 100,000 miles create a large step in a car's value?
entries.objective: Distinguish smooth wear from a discontinuity at an odometer's round-number boundary.
entries.sourceText: Used-car prices drop discretely each time the odometer crosses a 10,000-mile mark (Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, 2012).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish smooth wear from a discontinuity at an odometer's round-number boundary.

entries.title: The wine's price label
entries.hook: Would the same wine taste different under a different displayed price?
entries.objective: Separate an expectation-induced rating difference from a change in the liquid.
entries.sourceText: The same wine labeled $90 rather than $10 was rated more pleasant, and reward-related brain activity rose with it (Plassmann, O'Doherty, Shiv & Rangel, 2008).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate an expectation-induced rating difference from a change in the liquid.

entries.title: The fee appears at checkout
entries.hook: When do you first see the complete ticket price?
entries.objective: Compare all-in prices with delayed fee disclosure while holding total prices visible at the end.
entries.sourceText: On StubHub, showing fees only at checkout led buyers to spend about 21% more and buy about 14% more often (Blake, Moshary, Sweeney & Tadelis, 2021).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare all-in prices with delayed fee disclosure while holding total prices visible at the end.

entries.title: Broken pieces in the set
entries.hook: Would you price the same dinnerware sets differently alone and side by side?
entries.objective: Distinguish separate evaluation from joint comparison of total usable pieces.
entries.sourceText: Viewed alone, a 24-piece dinnerware set was valued at $33 versus $23 for a 40-piece set with some broken pieces; side by side, the larger set won (Hsee, 1998).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish separate evaluation from joint comparison of total usable pieces.

entries.title: The fine becomes a price
entries.hook: Would charging for late pickup make it feel permitted?
entries.objective: Separate a social obligation from a priced transaction and inspect persistence after removal.
entries.sourceText: After Israeli daycares introduced a fine for late pickup, late pickups nearly doubled and stayed high after the fine was removed (Gneezy & Rustichini, 2000).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate a social obligation from a priced transaction and inspect persistence after removal.

entries.title: A gift for a blood donor
entries.hook: Must every reward crowd out a prosocial action?
entries.objective: Contrast a gift-card field result with a blanket crowding-out rule.
entries.sourceText: Gift cards for Red Cross blood drives raised turnout without lowering donor quality (Lacetera, Macis & Slonim, 2012).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast a gift-card field result with a blanket crowding-out rule.

entries.title: Faster work, different workers
entries.hook: If output rises after piece pay, how much came from who joined?
entries.objective: Decompose an observed productivity increase into worker effort and workforce selection.
entries.sourceText: Switching Safelite windshield installers to piece rates raised productivity 44%, about half from attracting faster workers (Lazear, 2000).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Decompose an observed productivity increase into worker effort and workforce selection.

entries.title: Pay for grades or reading?
entries.hook: What changes if a reward targets an input instead of an outcome?
entries.objective: Compare controllable study inputs with final outcomes as incentive targets.
entries.sourceText: Paying students for grades did little, while paying them to read books raised scores (Fryer, 2011).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare controllable study inputs with final outcomes as incentive targets.

entries.title: The loan in cumulative dollars
entries.hook: Does a cumulative dollar bill tell a different story than a two-week fee?
entries.objective: Distinguish cost disclosure salience from a change in the loan's actual terms.
entries.sourceText: Showing payday borrowers the cumulative dollar cost of a loan cut borrowing about 11% (Bertrand & Morse, 2011).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish cost disclosure salience from a change in the loan's actual terms.

entries.title: A reminder at the right time
entries.hook: Could a savings reminder matter even without adding money?
entries.objective: Separate attention to a savings goal from a subsidy or higher return.
entries.sourceText: Simple text reminders raised savings about 6% in three countries (Karlan, McConnell, Mullainathan & Zinman, 2016).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate attention to a savings goal from a subsidy or higher return.

entries.title: Stop at the match cap?
entries.hook: Is the employer-match threshold also the right personal savings target?
entries.objective: Distinguish the incentive schedule's kink from a complete retirement decision.
entries.sourceText: Employees bunch their 401(k) contributions exactly at the employer-match cap (Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2002).
entries.sourcePointer: 500-behavioral-economics-findings.md entry 333: k; Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2002
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish the incentive schedule's kink from a complete retirement decision.

entries.title: Your colleague went to the fair
entries.hook: Could an invitation affect people who never received it?
entries.objective: Identify spillovers to colleagues and distinguish them from direct treatment effects.
entries.sourceText: Inviting university staff to a benefits fair, with a small payment, raised retirement plan enrollment, also among their colleagues (Duflo & Saez, 2003).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Identify spillovers to colleagues and distinguish them from direct treatment effects.

entries.title: Write a date and time
entries.hook: Would you leave the vaccination plan vague or put it on the calendar?
entries.objective: Distinguish intention strength from an implementation plan with a concrete time.
entries.sourceText: Prompting employees to write down the date and time they'd get a flu shot raised vaccination 4.2 percentage points (Milkman, Beshears, Choi, Laibson & Madrian, 2011).
entries.sourcePointer: 500-behavioral-economics-findings.md entry 342: Milkman, Beshears, Choi, Laibson & Madrian, 2011
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish intention strength from an implementation plan with a concrete time.

entries.title: Return after the missed visit
entries.hook: Which reward would you test after a workout streak breaks?
entries.objective: Compare interventions aimed at recovery after a lapse with rewards for maintaining a perfect streak.
entries.sourceText: In a megastudy of 54 gym interventions with 61,000 members, small bonuses for returning after a missed workout worked best, and experts predicted results poorly (Milkman et al., 2021).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare interventions aimed at recovery after a lapse with rewards for maintaining a perfect streak.

entries.title: More program, more adherence?
entries.hook: Does a multi-part intervention guarantee a measurable improvement?
entries.objective: Distinguish intervention complexity from evidence of benefit in a randomized result.
entries.sourceText: A multi-part behavioral program for heart-attack patients' medication adherence had no effect (Volpp et al., 2017).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish intervention complexity from evidence of benefit in a randomized result.

entries.title: Hour one or hour twelve?
entries.hook: Does a whole-shift average hide a decline in hand-hygiene compliance?
entries.objective: Read changes across the shift without inferring that time alone caused the difference.
entries.sourceText: Hospital caregivers' hand-hygiene compliance fell 8.7 percentage points over a 12-hour shift (Dai, Milkman, Hofmann & Staats, 2015).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Read changes across the shift without inferring that time alone caused the difference.

entries.sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
entries.title: The court letter's next step
entries.hook: Would a clearer summons and a reminder change missed appearances?
entries.objective: Distinguish ability to act on a notice from fear of the underlying penalty.
entries.sourceText: Redesigned court summonses and text reminders cut missed court dates in New York by 13–21% (Fishbane, Ouss & Shah, 2020).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish ability to act on a notice from fear of the underlying penalty.

entries.sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
entries.title: A letter or hands-on help?
entries.hook: How much does application help add beyond information alone?
entries.objective: Compare control, information, and assisted-application arms as separate interventions.
entries.sourceText: SNAP enrollment among eligible seniors was 6% with no contact, 11% with an information letter and 18% with help applying (Finkelstein & Notowidigdo, 2019).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare control, information, and assisted-application arms as separate interventions.

entries.sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
entries.title: Fuel information, then the purchase
entries.hook: Does giving personalized fuel costs guarantee a different car purchase?
entries.objective: Distinguish an information treatment from evidence that the final choice changed.
entries.sourceText: Giving car shoppers personalized fuel-cost information did not change which cars they bought (Allcott & Knittel, 2019).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish an information treatment from evidence that the final choice changed.

entries.sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
entries.title: The conflict is disclosed
entries.hook: Does a conflict warning automatically remove biased advice?
entries.objective: Separate disclosure from adviser behavior and recipient adjustment.
entries.sourceText: Advisors who disclosed a conflict of interest gave more biased advice, and recipients didn't discount it enough (Cain, Loewenstein & Moore, 2005).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate disclosure from adviser behavior and recipient adjustment.

entries.title: More shifts, less effort
entries.hook: Can total labor supply rise while effort per shift falls?
entries.objective: Separate the extensive margin of taking shifts from within-shift effort.
entries.sourceText: Zurich bike messengers worked more shifts when pay rose but put in less effort per shift (Fehr & Goette, 2007).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate the extensive margin of taking shifts from within-shift effort.

entries.title: No raise, but no pay cut
entries.hook: Why might wage changes pile up at exactly zero?
entries.objective: Read a zero mass in a distribution without confusing nominal and real pay changes.
entries.sourceText: Wage-change data show a spike at exactly zero, since employers rarely cut nominal pay (Card & Hyslop, 1997; Kahn, 1997).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Read a zero mass in a distribution without confusing nominal and real pay changes.

entries.title: The ad says negotiable
entries.hook: Would stating a negotiation rule change who opens a negotiation?
entries.objective: Contrast ambiguity about negotiability with an explicit common rule.
entries.sourceText: When job ads stated wages were negotiable, the gender gap in negotiating disappeared (Leibbrandt & List, 2015).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast ambiguity about negotiability with an explicit common rule.

entries.title: Two days at home
entries.hook: Could retention improve without a measured performance increase?
entries.objective: Distinguish worker-retention outcomes from performance outcomes in the hybrid-work trial.
entries.sourceText: Hybrid work two days a week left performance unchanged and cut quits by a third (Bloom, Han & Liang, 2024).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish worker-retention outcomes from performance outcomes in the hybrid-work trial.

entries.title: The Friday earnings report
entries.hook: Would the same news receive the same immediate reaction on Friday?
entries.objective: Separate the timing of attention from the direction of the earnings information.
entries.sourceText: Earnings announced on Fridays get a weaker immediate reaction and more later drift (DellaVigna & Pollet, 2009).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate the timing of attention from the direction of the earnings information.

entries.title: MCI or MCIC?
entries.hook: Could one company's news move an unrelated ticker?
entries.objective: Distinguish name similarity from a shared claim on company cash flows.
entries.sourceText: Shares of a small fund with ticker MCI moved with news about the telecom MCI Communications, whose ticker was MCIC (Rashes, 2001).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish name similarity from a shared claim on company cash flows.

entries.title: The company down the road
entries.hook: Would a nearby headquarters change a fund manager's portfolio weight?
entries.objective: Distinguish local geographic familiarity from national home-country preference.
entries.sourceText: US fund managers overweight companies headquartered nearby (Coval & Moskowitz, 1999).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish local geographic familiarity from national home-country preference.

entries.title: Open the account after a loss?
entries.hook: Would a market drop change when you choose to look at your portfolio?
entries.objective: Separate attention to an outcome from the investment outcome itself.
entries.sourceText: Investors look up their portfolios less after market declines, the "ostrich effect" (Karlsson, Loewenstein & Seppi, 2009).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate attention to an outcome from the investment outcome itself.

entries.title: A longer cold-water trial
entries.hook: Would you repeat a longer trial if it ended more gently?
entries.objective: Contrast accumulated discomfort with retrospective choice influenced by the ending.
entries.sourceText: After holding a hand in cold water for 60 seconds, and separately for 90 seconds ending slightly warmer, 69% chose to repeat the longer trial (Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, 1993).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast accumulated discomfort with retrospective choice influenced by the ending.

entries.title: Winners a decade later
entries.hook: Does an early small study settle what lottery wins do to satisfaction?
entries.objective: Distinguish the larger long-run lottery evidence from the blanket adaptation claim.
entries.sourceText: Large Swedish lottery winners reported higher life satisfaction for over a decade (Lindqvist, Östling & Cesarini, 2020).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish the larger long-run lottery evidence from the blanket adaptation claim.

entries.title: Buy a thing, or buy time?
entries.hook: Would you spend the same money on an item or on avoiding a chore?
entries.objective: Separate spending amount from the kind of benefit being purchased.
entries.sourceText: Paying for time-saving services raised life satisfaction more than buying goods (Whillans et al., 2017).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate spending amount from the kind of benefit being purchased.

entries.title: Silver or bronze?
entries.hook: Would second place always feel better than third?
entries.objective: Distinguish absolute rank from the comparison outcome someone may imagine.
entries.sourceText: Olympic bronze medalists looked happier than silver medalists (Medvec, Madey & Gilovich, 1995).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish absolute rank from the comparison outcome someone may imagine.

entries.title: The private die report
entries.hook: Can a distribution reveal excess high reports without identifying a liar?
entries.objective: Distinguish aggregate reporting evidence from accusations about individual participants.
entries.sourceText: When people privately rolled a die and reported the result for pay, about 20% lied to the maximum and 39% were fully honest (Fischbacher & Föllmi-Heusi, 2013).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish aggregate reporting evidence from accusations about individual participants.

entries.title: Who pays for the lie?
entries.hook: Would the same personal gain feel different if another person lost more?
entries.objective: Separate the liar's gain from the cost imposed on the recipient.
entries.sourceText: People lie less when the lie costs the other person more (Gneezy, 2005).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate the liar's gain from the cost imposed on the recipient.

entries.title: Who reports the income?
entries.hook: Would third-party records change the opportunity for tax evasion?
entries.objective: Contrast third-party and self-reported income without treating their association as an individual moral trait.
entries.sourceText: Danish tax evasion was about 0.3% of income reported by employers or banks, versus about 37% of self-reported income (Kleven et al., 2011).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Contrast third-party and self-reported income without treating their association as an individual moral trait.

entries.title: Can anyone see the report?
entries.hook: Would a visible false report feel the same as a private one?
entries.objective: Distinguish observability of dishonesty from the material payoff to lying.
entries.sourceText: People lie less when others can see the lie (Gneezy, Kajackaite & Sobel, 2018).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish observability of dishonesty from the material payoff to lying.

entries.title: Years of data, one missing variable
entries.hook: Can experience teach an effect you never notice or vary?
entries.objective: Distinguish accumulated observations from attention to the yield-relevant input.
entries.sourceText: Indonesian seaweed farmers ignored pod size, which mattered for yield, despite years of their own data (Hanna, Mullainathan & Schwartzstein, 2014).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish accumulated observations from attention to the yield-relevant input.

entries.title: The bat and the ball
entries.hook: A bat and ball cost $1.10; the bat costs $1 more. What is the ball's price?
entries.objective: Check an intuitive answer against both simultaneous price constraints.
entries.sourceText: Only 17% of 3,428 people answered all three Cognitive Reflection Test questions right; most said the ball costs 10 cents (Frederick, 2005).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Check an intuitive answer against both simultaneous price constraints.

entries.title: The warmer school year
entries.hook: Does a temperature-learning association look the same with cooling available?
entries.objective: Distinguish environmental exposure from its moderation by air conditioning.
entries.sourceText: A school year 1°F hotter, without air conditioning, reduced learning about 1% (Park, Goodman, Hurwitz & Smith, 2020).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish environmental exposure from its moderation by air conditioning.

entries.title: Paid early, then the workday
entries.hook: Could wage timing affect output before total pay changes?
entries.objective: Separate short-term liquidity from the total wage and inspect indebtedness as a moderator.
entries.sourceText: Paying Indian workers part of their wages early raised productivity, especially among the most indebted (Kaur, Mullainathan, Oh & Schilbach, 2021).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Separate short-term liquidity from the total wage and inspect indebtedness as a moderator.

entries.sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
entries.title: One hundred studies, two passes
entries.hook: What does a 36% significant-replication rate actually count?
entries.objective: Distinguish a significant replication count from a claim that the remaining effects are all exactly zero.
entries.sourceText: Only about 36% of 100 published psychology findings replicated with significant results (Open Science Collaboration, 2015).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish a significant replication count from a claim that the remaining effects are all exactly zero.

entries.sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
entries.title: Eleven of eighteen
entries.hook: Would you compare replication percentages without their sample sizes?
entries.objective: Translate 11 of 18 into a proportion and state its limited experiment sample.
entries.sourceText: 11 of 18 lab experiments in top economics journals replicated, about 61% (Camerer et al., 2016).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Translate 11 of 18 into a proportion and state its limited experiment sample.

entries.sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
entries.title: The replicated effect shrinks
entries.hook: Can a result replicate while the estimated effect becomes smaller?
entries.objective: Distinguish direction or significance replication from equality of effect size.
entries.sourceText: 13 of 21 social science experiments in *Nature* and *Science* replicated, with effects about half their original size (Camerer et al., 2018).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Distinguish direction or significance replication from equality of effect size.

entries.sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
entries.title: Bet before the rerun
entries.hook: How could you test whether forecasts identify replicable studies?
entries.objective: Compare forecasts recorded before replication with later outcomes rather than hindsight explanations.
entries.sourceText: Researchers betting in prediction markets forecast which studies would replicate better than chance (Dreber et al., 2015).
entries.meaningfulDifference: Compare forecasts recorded before replication with later outcomes rather than hindsight explanations.
